newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia faces LNG glut, demand views unrealistic.
newsitem.headline: Asia faces LNG glut, demand views unrealistic.

text.p: Unrealistic official demand projections for liquefied natural gas (LNG) in Asia could lead to a supply surplus, the Honolulu-based think tank East-West Centre said on Thursday.

"Despite the variability in Asia's gas demand outlook, base case scenarios suggest mounting pressure towards a surplus in LNG supply," Fereidun Fesharaki, a director of the East-West Centre told the Asian Gas conference in Singapore.
He said that even under the highest projections for demand, some discussed gas supply projects would not be needed until after 2010.
Fesharaki said was included projects in Yemen, Sakhalin, Papua New Guinea, Canada, Alaska and the Natuna and Wiriagar fields in Indonesia under this heading.
Projection for low demand made the risks of over supply even worse, he said.
But Fesharaki said he expected some expansion projects to be needed, including Malaysian LNG III, Qatar's Ras Lafan II and additional capacity in Oman and Australia.
"Governments, especially Japan, may exaggerate future LNG imports in order to demonstrate desirable reductions in carbon dioxide and polluting emissions," he said.
Fesharaki said gas made up a smaller share of Asia's energy sector than in the rest of the world.
Excluding China and India, Asia's production of commercial gas was comparable to the world average, but consumption remained low, he said.
Overestimates of nuclear power supply and political volatility were adding uncertainty to forecasts of Asia's gas market, he added.
"The choices made by some countries such as Japan and South Korea for meeting electricity needs that will not be supplied by nuclear power could increase future gas trade," he said.
"But there is also downward pressure on gas trade, stemming from lower than expected economic growth or political olatility."
Fesharaki cited South Korea as an example.
"South Korea is Asia's fastest growing gas consumer but military conflict or reunification with North Korea could restrain its growing gas trade if not its entire economy," he said.
